INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
This amicus curiae brief is filed on behalf of the Hawaii
Firearms Coalition in support of petitioners. Hawaii
Firearms Coalition (HIFICO), is a non-profit, member
driven organization incorporated under the laws of the
State of Hawaii with its principal place of business in
Honolulu Hawaii, dedicated to the correct construction,
interpretation, and application of the law 1 and which
promotes legislative and legal action, as well as research,
and advocacy, in support of people’s civil liberties.
Hawaii Firearms Coalition litigates firearm-regulation
cases, and it has consistently advocated for a principled
interpretation of the United States Constitution to prevent
government from violating the basic civil rights of its
citizens. Members of HIFICO have provided informed
analysis and been organizational plaintiffs in a variety of
firearm related cases, including Fisher vs. Louis Kealoha,
et al., 855 F . 3d 1067 (9th Cir. 2017), Roberts vs. City and
County of Honolulu , Civ. No. 15-00467 ACK-RLP, and
Roberts vs. Ballard, et al., Civ. No. 18-00125, and Wolford
et al. v Anne E. Lopez , 1:23-cv-00265. Hawaii Firearm
Coalition’s interest in this matter is for this Court to come
to the correct interpretation of the Second Amendment
such that all members of the people may exercise the
Second Amendment completely and as applicable to this
case, that the arms include, “any thing that a man wears
for his defense, or takes into his hands, or used in wrath
to cast at or strike another.”, and that there is no well-
1. No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or
in part, nor did such counsel or any party make a monetary
contribution to fund this brief. No person other than the amicus,
its members or counsel, made a monetary contribution intended
to fund the preparation or submission of this brief.

2
established and enduring historical tradition of banning
arms that could contribute to the efficiency of the militia
and or could be useful in case of confrontation.
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
This Court should find that the arms at issue in this
litigation are of the kind and nature that have a reasonable
relationship to the preservation or efficiency of the militia
and are of the sort that militia members are expected to
possess, train with, and carry for confrontation whether
while in militia service or in defense of themselves and
others. As will be shown below, “arms” include, not only
“militia” or “military” weapons, but any weapon of offense.
ARGUMENT
Amicus begins by stating that Amicus agrees with
Petitioners’ arguments regarding the “in common use”
aspect of the arms in question. Additionally, Amicus
agrees not only with Petitioners’ arguments regarding
the “…historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of
dangerous and unusual weapons…”, (Emphasis added), 2
but also the more precise and thorough argument of
Amicus Hawaii Rifle Association, filed August 31, 2026,
that ties the “historical tradition” of “…prohibiting the
carrying of dangerous and unusual weapons…” to the act
of how a weapon was employed, not the mere possession or
ownership of the weapon, nor any intrinsic characteristic
of the arm. Furthermore, under the Heller framework,
as explicated by Bruen, Amicus argues that any and all
“arms” or any “weapons of offence of armour of defence”3
2. See Petitioners’ brief filed August 28, 2026, pages 43-46.
3. Heller at 627.

3
are included in step one of Bruen, as implicated in the text
of the Second Amendment, and whether or not there is a
tradition of regulation is addressed at step two, examining
the history and tradition.
Writing for the Court in District of Columbia v.
Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 595-596, (2008), Justice Scalia,
while determining that the Second Amendment was an
individual right, discussed that the individual bore arms,
in part, as a member of the “militia”.
The militia of a country are the able bodied
men organized into companies, regiments
and brigades… and required by law to attend
military exercises on certain days only, but
at other times left to pursue their usual
occupations.”
…
…the militia of the State, that is to say, of every
man in it able to bear arms”.
But to what end? For what purposes does the
individual keep and bear arms 4? Heller informed us that,
at base, the Second Amendment protects the right to keep
and bear arms as follows—
4. And exercise all aspects related to the “keeping” and
bearing”, such as making, purchasing, trading, modifying, training,
practicing, buying bags, training equipment, ammunition, targets,
optics, hearing protection, cleaning materials, holsters, storage
boxes, safes, hunting, plinking, target shooting, competitive
shooting, establishing collections, etc, all beyond “individual” or
group, confrontation.

4
“When used with “arms,” however, the term
has a meaning that refers to carrying for a
particular purpose—confrontation.”
“Putting all of these textual elements together,
we find that they guarantee the individual
right to possess and carry weapons in case of
confrontation.”
Heller at 5845, 592.
But since 1791, governmental efforts to abolish or
strangle Second Amendment rights, have shifted gears. In
Heller6, the government sought to restrict Heller’s access to
a pistol7. Yet, in Heller, the court discussed how the Second
Amendment was not limited to the protection of weapons
of militia service. The Second Amendment is expansive,
5. Also see 594.
6. Heller  discussed how the government had sought to
limit the militia to select militias. Heller at 592, 598, 600. That
effort remains today with government trying to limit the Second
Amendment by limiting who is covered by “the people”. The
courts and governments most resistant to Bruen, try to smuggle
in restrictions at step one, instead of looking at the history and
tradition in step two, as Bruen dictates. This effort to avoid Bruen,
or the mistake in applying Bruen, is the second prong, the first
is to limit the persons covered in the Second Amendment, the
second is to just eliminate large categories of arms, purportedly,
at step one.
7. Heller at 574-575. The dissent, then argued, that pistols
were associated with criminals and crime, and therefore were
not “militia” service related. Here, the government takes the
approach that the arms are too close to militia related, i.e. they are
too dangerous and unusual ( a misapplication of the term of art).

5
covering “confrontation” in all its forms8. “Confrontation”
covers protection everything from individual assailants to
assisting in the defense of one’s country.
Heller explained, and Bruen explicated, that the text
of the Second Amendment controls and covers “arms”.
Heller “…defined ‘arms’ as ‘ any thing that a man wears
for his defense, or takes into his hands, or used in wrath
to cast at or strike another.” (Emphasis added). A broad
definition indeed. And to make clear, Heller added “…all
firearms constituted ‘arms’… Heller at 581. (Emphasis
added). Heller continued “…the second Amendment
extends, prima facie, to all instruments  that constitute
bearable arms, …” (Emphasis added).
Beyond that very broad scope, a distinct, but not
limiting, aspect of the Second Amendment was militia
service. Heller explained, at 585, “It is clear from those
formulations that “bear arms” did not refer only to
carrying a weapon in an organized military unit.”
While that discussion in Heller was, in that specific
paragraph, discussing the “people” and the fact that
keeping and bearing “arms” was not limited to militia
service, it begs the question, what sort of “arm” did
the individual keep and bear, not only for individual
confrontation, but also for “militia service”?
Justice Scalia noted, at 602, “19 th century courts
never read common defence to limit the use of weapons
to militia service.” (Emphasis added). In addressing the
minimal impact of the Miller case, Justice Scalia noted,
8. Caetano, 577 U.S. 411 (2016).

6
at 622, “…the Second Amendment confers an individual
right to keep and bear arms…that have some reasonable
relationship to the preservation or efficiency of a well
regulated militia.”
Miller itself, was not a challenge to the specific arm,
or characteristic of an arm, in question, because it was
instead merely an odd case 9 about the “…transporting
9. In fact it was not only odd but suspicious because it was
essentially the government that crafted it to be a test case to
determine whether arms could be almost banned through the
tax power under the constitution, recognizing, and implicitly
admitting, that the government could not directly ban the
weapons, and arguing instead that the registration and taxation
was aimed at persons who committed crimes, by applying the
tax to weapons that criminals liked to use. The government
argued that the weapons might not be “protected” because they
were used by criminals, an argument foreclosed by Heller. The
Supreme Court dodged that precise question and noted that the
arm, a short-barreled shotgun, was not, as a matter of judicial
notice, part of ordinary military equipment or could contribute
to the common defense. The implication is that if there had been
some evidence, any evidence, or argument (the precise evidentiary
question was not raised in the trial court) that a shorter barreled
shotgun was a part of ordinary military equipment, that a member
of the militia brought himself, or could contribute to the common
defense, then the analysis would have been very different. Even
that examination is suspect considering Bruen’s explication that if
the plain text of the Second Amendment covers the issue, “an arm”,
then the burden falls to the government to establish a tradition
of regulation. And even the Miller court considered the shorter
barreled shotgun to be an “arm”. The government argued the
“arm” could be regulated not because of what it was, intrinsically,
but rather by whom it was being used. It did not argue that it
was not an “arm”- though the case focused on “short” barreled
shotguns, the Tommy Gun machine gun, also covered by the NFA,

7
an unregistered  short-barreled shotgun…”, Heller at
621-622. (Emphasis added)(It was the fact that it was
“unregistered”, not that it was “short-barreled”, and
transported in interstate commerce, that constituted the
crime. Shotguns without short barrels were not required
to be “registered”, and if they were unregistered they were
legal to possess and lawfully use. And even short-barreled
shotguns were legal to buy, possess, own and use, provided
it was “registered”. If “registered” they must have had
some use for self-defense, and perhaps militia service.) It
was not a real challenge because no one showed up to make
the challenge.10 See The Peculiar Story of United States v
Miller, NY Journal of Law and Liberty, Vol. 3, 2008. Miller
did not address, nor even raise the issue of, an arm being
“dangerous and unusual” as it pertained to the weapon
at issue, that was “unregistered”, such weapon being a
was in fact used by the Postal Service and United States Marines
to guard the mail in the 1920’s, see https://postalmuseum.si.edu/
object/npm_2013.2011.158, last accessed September 2, 2026.
10. See Heller, footnote 25. In discussing the decision in
Lewis v. United States, 445 U.S. 55, 100 S.Ct. 915, 63 L.Ed.2d
198 (1980), which in turn discussed Miller, Justice Scalia noted
“It is inconceivable that we would rest our interpretation of the
basic meaning of any guarantee of the Bill of Rights upon such
a footnoted dictum in a case where the point was not at issue
and was not argued.” Here, similarly, Heller  was not about
“dangerous and unusual weapons”. And Miller, did not decide
anything about “dangerous and unusual” weapons, in part because
the concept, issue and argument was never raised, and because
one party didn’t make any argument at all. But also because, as
explained in Amicus Hawaii Rifle Association’s brief, the concept
of “dangerous and unusual” meant how an arm was carried- and
being “unregistered” was not “to the terror” of the people, nor
was a weapon being “short”.

8
“short barreled shotgun”11. The Miller court, importantly,
considered the “short barreled shotgun” an “arm”, thus
it would be covered and the NFA would be implicated
by the text of the Second Amendment. The Miller court
simply stated “…it is not within judicial notice 12 that this
weapon is any part of the ordinary military equipment…”.
That meant, whether or not the arm could be regulated
in some way, was connected to its service in the militia
or common defense.
It should be noted that as to the precise question
of whether or not a short-barreled shotgun had any
“reasonable relationship to the preservation or efficiency
of the …militia”, or was “… any part…of the ordinary
military equipment or that its use could contribute  to
the common defense.”, (Emphasis added), that question
was not necessary for the underlying indictment, criminal
charge and, since no one appeared to argue on behalf of
Miller, was not addressed at the U.S. Supreme Court in
argument by Miller.
Despite the exceedingly shallow nature of Miller, and
the fact that Heller all but disregarded it, (in response to
the dissent), Justice Scalia pointed out at 623, that the
government, in Heller, argued, “…for the proposition that
the only uses of arms protected by the Second Amendment
11. What constitutes “short” in a shotgun is completely
arbitrary and does not eliminate the utility of a shorter shotgun
from militia or self-defense applications or use.
12. Judicial notice can be used to accept that international
law exists. See The Paquete Habana, 175 U.S. 677 (1900). But facts
applicable to an item, such as a short-barreled shotgun, specific
facts, are the kinds of facts that cannot be judicially noticed, See
Garner v State of LA, 368 U.S. 157 (1961).

9
are those that relate to the militia, not self-defense 13.”
This was to support the government’s position, to use
the Miller14 case as a National Firearm Act test case
to use the NFA to prosecute specific types of criminals,
i.e. “gangsters”, that short-barreled guns are associated
with crimes and used by criminals. But, as Justice Scalia
noted in discussing Miller, at 624, “It assumes from the
prologue that the Amendment was designed to preserve
the militia.” And Heller ruled that even if an arm is used
by criminals, it does not mean that it falls out of the text
of the Second Amendment, nor that it necessarily has a
history and tradition of regulation 15 or a ban of the arm (
as opposed to the possession by a particular person). See
Heller at 636 –
“We are aware of the problem of handgun violence in
this country, and we take seriously the concerns raised by
the many amici who believe that prohibition of handgun
ownership is a solution. The Constitution leaves the
District of Columbia a variety of tools for combating that
problem, including some measures regulating handguns,
see supra, at 2816 – 2817, and n. 26. But the enshrinement
of constitutional rights necessarily takes certain policy
13. And it is now well-established, under Heller , that
general confrontation is what is, also, protected under the Second
Amendment.
14. But Miller itself was not about the mere possession or
existence of a short-barreled shotgun, or a weapon with certain
characteristics, but rather it was “registered” because the
government knew, criminals would not register an arm, while a law
abiding person would. The NFA had originally sought to include
pistols, see FN 19, page 17. So, they too, were used by criminals.
15. Putting aside other regulation of arms generally such
as a prohibition of using an arm, any arm, to commit robbery or
homicide.

10
choices off the table. These include the absolute prohibition
of handguns held and used for self-defense in the home.
Undoubtedly some think that the Second Amendment
is outmoded in a society where our standing army is the
pride of our Nation, where well-trained police forces
provide personal security, and where gun violence is a
serious problem. That is perhaps debatable, but what
is not debatable is that it is not the role of this Court to
pronounce the Second Amendment extinct 16”.
Many courts have inappropriately stretched
discussion, not ruling, in Heller, twisted it, and avoided a
proper Bruen analysis as it pertains to “machine guns”
and, accordingly, other “arms”. In Viramontes, 2025 WL
1553896, the court wrote “We held that the plaintiffs had
failed to show, at the preliminary injunction stage, that the
covered firearms materially differed from machineguns
and military-grade weaponry, which the Supreme
Court instructed can be banned under the Second
Amendment. Id. at 1194–97, 1203.” (Emphasis added).
The Heller court stated no such thing.
First, the Heller court was dealing with a handgun
ban17. The language most often cited for the proposition to
16. Amicus notes that the “assault rifles” at issue here, are,
as shown by Petitioners, owned in the millions, and handguns, as
indicated in Heller, “…are the most popular weapon chosen by
Americans for self defense in the home,…”, at 629. As Petitioners
note, at 2, “It did not matter, as a dissent emphasized, that
handguns also are “the overwhelmingly favorite weapon of armed
criminals.” This argument, that only criminals use a certain type
of weapon, was raised in support of the NFA, and in Miller, but
was not dispositive, and was ruled as irrelevant in Heller.
17. Handguns too can be “militia” or “military” grade, or
“style” weaponry, but the 7 th Circuit’s main focus was on the

11
ban weapons, such as so-called “assault” rifles, which was
not a part of the issue decided in Heller, at 627-628, is –
“It may be objected that if weapons that are most
useful in military service—M–16 rifles and the like—
may be banned, then the Second Amendment right is
completely detached from the prefatory clause. But as
we have said, the conception of the militia at the time of
the Second Amendment’s ratification was the body of all
citizens capable of military service, who would bring the
sorts of lawful weapons that they possessed at home 18 to
“rifles” at issue with “features” such as a thumbhole stock,
folding or telescoping stock, flash suppressor, and the like. One
feature, “pistol grip” would obviously be applicable to all or
almost all pistols. See https://nationalinterest.org/blog/buzz/
ultimate-mistake-introducing-gun-us-army-said-no-39502,
last accessed September 2, 2026, an article that notes that the
M9, civilian version 92F, Beretta 9mm pistol was the United
States Army’s pistol since 1985 for more than thirty years. That
same pistol, with miniscule differences, has been available to
civilians, from initial production. See https://www.craftholsters.
com/beretta-m9-vs-92fs-side-by-side-comparison-of-berettasbest?srsltid=AfmBOoqAZLNcZfD7zjY0-5f3A4WJ8J8hya3kjgV
FleR1vqsDxReWS5XN, last accessed September 2, 2026.
18. Amicus notes that Petitioners have ably proven that
millions of Americans owns millions of AR15 platform style rifles.
Amicus notes that as far as fully automatic firearms, covered
by the National Firearms Act (NFA) of 1934 is concerned,
prior to the enactment of the NFA, fully automatic firearms,
unregistered, were in ample supply in the country. See https://
www.americanrifleman.org/content/guns-of-the-battle-of-blairmountain/, last accessed September 1, 2026. This article describes
the battle of Blair mountain in 1921. The article describes
miners, civilians, “… volunteers showed up with an unimaginable
assortment of their own guns. Civilian hunting rifles, shotguns and
handguns of all makes, models, calibers and gauges are described
in the accounts of the period, as too are surplus obsolescent
military arms (including some foreign designs), and even some

12
militia duty. It may well be true today that a militia, to be
as effective as militias in the 18th century, would require
sophisticated arms that are highly unusual in society at
large19. Indeed, it may be true that no amount of small
arms could be useful against modern-day bombers and
tanks. But the fact that modern developments have limited
the degree of fit between the prefatory clause *628 and
the protected right cannot change our interpretation of
the right.”
That language is not a definitive ruling that “M-16’s”,
“and the like’” “may be banned” 20. Important language
muzzleloaders. In addition, there were large numbers of Thompson
submachine guns, as well as Winchester Model 1897 riot shotguns,
available to the Logan County Defenders. American Legionnaires
carried the surplus U.S. Krag rifles that had been distributed to
Legion posts nationwide by the U.S. government only the year
before. Mine-company-owned Colt-Browning “potato digger”
machine guns  were pressed into service, and there are reports
of Gatling guns and perhaps even some then-current U.S.-issue
automatic arms  being used …” (Emphasis added).
19. This speculation by Justice Scalia is unsupported and
unjustified by actual records. Again, Heller  did not address
or make any rulings with regard to fully automatic weapons.
Justice Scalia “ presumed” for the sake of argument, that M-16’s
“may be banned” and that the NFA “might” be constitutional, or
unconstitutional. Despite the NFA, which doesn’t per se “ban” fully
automatic weapons, it merely requires them to be “registered”
and a tax paid with them, Americans own more than 782,958
